title: The Sleep Revolution
note: Full subtitle: Transforming Your Life, One Night at a Time. Full text not read; facts come from Huffington's own words in interviews given for the book launch and from reviews.

facts.claim: 'On the morning of April 6, 2007, I was lying on the floor of my home office in a pool of blood.' On her way down her head hit the corner of her desk; she broke her cheekbone. She had collapsed from exhaustion and sleep deprivation.
facts.source: Huffington in amerisleep interview; Fortune; WTTW

facts.claim: For the two years she was building The Huffington Post she worked regular 18-hour days.

Afterwards she went 'from doctor to doctor, from brain MRI to CAT scan to echocardiogram' to rule out an underlying condition; 'doctors' waiting rooms, it turns out, were good places for me to ask myself a lot of questions.'
She names the belief at the heart of the sleep crisis: that 'overwork and burnout are the price we must pay in order to succeed'; going without sleep is treated as 'a badge of honor'.
The book covers how common sleep deprivation is, especially among professionals and college students, warns about sleep medications such as Ambien, and urges seven to eight hours a night.
Her top recommendation: get all devices out of the bedroom. She turns them off at a set time each night and 'gently escort[s] them out of my bedroom'.

She treats the transition to sleep as 'a sacrosanct ritual': a hot bath with Epsom salts and a candle flickering nearby; she no longer sleeps in workout clothes but in pajamas, nightdresses or T-shirts dedicated to sleep; sometimes chamomile or lavender tea.
Huffington installed nap rooms at The Huffington Post; staff were reluctant at first, then the rooms were 'perpetually full'. She predicted nap rooms would become as common as conference rooms.
The 'two legs of a stool' image (money and power) and the Third Metric of well-being, wisdom, wonder and giving come from her earlier book Thrive (2014), not from The Sleep Revolution.
facts.source: Penguin Random House and Porchlight descriptions of Thrive

facts.claim: Huffington admits she did not realize the importance of sleep until 2007 and says: 'I don't want you to make the mistakes I did.'

rejected.claim: Quote 'If this is what success looks like, what does failure look like?' as said in the moment.
rejected.reason: Not found in reachable sources for this book; dropped.

rejected.claim: Quote 'We need a third revolution, a sleep and well-being revolution, next to the business and technology revolutions.'
Screens off 30 minutes before bed, light book, dimmed lights as her exact system; 'the bath is the transition ritual between day and night' quote.
rejected.reason: The 30 minutes and the quote are not sourced; the ritual is reported in her own words without them.

rejected.claim: Eight hours of poor sleep is less useful than six hours of deep sleep; quality is decided in the hour before bed.
rejected.reason: No source; contradicts her 7-8 hours advice.

rejected.claim: Two-legged stool, wisdom, wonder, generosity as success pillars; 'a company that lets staff work on sleep debt writes letters with a blunt pencil'.
rejected.reason: The stool and pillars belong to Thrive (2014); the pencil quote has no source.

1339.note: Collapse story kept; invented quotes removed; the doctors' tests and waiting-room questions added.

1340.note: Bedtime ritual rebuilt from her own words; invented 30 minutes and 8-vs-6-hours claim dropped.

1341.note: The central idea (success as a stool with more legs, well-being/wisdom/wonder/giving) is from Thrive, a different book; the workplace quote is unsourced.
